This study introduces the Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with Exogenous covariates (TV-P) and Time-Varying Poisson PARX (TV-PARX) models, extending recent work by Cao and Yang (2019) to accommodate nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. We derive explicit time-varyying coefficient estimates and formulate practical tests for structural breaks within the TV-P framework. Using a smoothing spline approach, we investigate the asymptotic properties of the resulting smoothed coefficient processes. Specifically, we prove that these processes converge weakly to a nonparametric diffusion process with time-varying drift and diffusion coefficients. Closed-form expressions are provided for the generator of this limiting diffusion. These findings enable precise tracking of how exogenous covariates influence response variables over time. Employing spline smoothing for asymptotic analysis represents a distinct methodological shift from conventional practices in time series research, which typically rely on spline approximations solely for constructing tests and estimating nonparametric functions, rather than for deriving asymptotic results. The proposed TV-P and TV-PARX models find extensive application in analyzing nonstationary count data exhibiting nonlinear patterns, structural shifts, and time-varying effects of covariates. Empirical evaluations through simulated examples and a real-world case study illustrate the construction, implementation, and practical utility of these methods. Additionally, open-source R code for these techniques is accessible at https://github.com/wenhaozhang1995/TVPcount.
This study demonstrates that high-precision, uncalibrated relative photometry via wide-field imaging serves as an effective method for monitoring changes in vertical aerosol optical depth ($z$-AOD) when absolute calibration is unnecessary. Utilizing two years of relative calibrations derived from star observations, we analyzed nine months of uncalibrated wide-field photometry collected by the GOES-16 Cloud and Aerosol Imager (CAI). This data was compared with concurrent AOD measurements from the NASA DC-8 aircraft and the AERONET network. The results indicate that relative photometry offers precision sufficient to detect diurnal and synoptic variations in z-AOD, achieving an root-mean-square (RMS) agreement of 0.01 with independent sources. Although z-AOD exhibited seasonal fluctuations, the CAI's monthly precision remained consistent at approximately 0.015. We conclude that this approach is particularly beneficial for cloud and aerosol imagers on weather satellites, providing a simple technique to enhance data quality and utility, provided absolute calibration through radiometric standards is not required. Furthermore, this strategy can be applied to past datasets from satellite imagers lacking prior absolute calibration, potentially improving their utility without reprocessing the original data. To implement this approach, we provide a set of simple guidelines in the supplementary materials.
This study evaluates the computational performance and accuracy of several numerical schemes—Lagrangian, Eulerian, and hybrid molecular dynamics (MD)—within large-scale biomolecular simulations using the alanine dipeptide. We implement a novel, highly performant numerical finite element method (FEM) via an Eulerian grid approach on an unstructured adaptive grid constructed from a cubic supergrid and its octants. Simulation accuracy is assessed by comparing configurations obtained using varying spatial discretizations against those from a high-precision Lagrangian MD run. Results indicate that the traditional Eulerian FEM yields significantly lower computational costs than the uncoupled numerical finite difference method. Furthermore, the proposed hybrid FEM demonstrates cost advantages over the Lagrangian approach at equivalent spatial resolutions, offering additional benefits at coarser grids. These simulations were executed using AMBER16 modified with NumPy's ufunc broadcasting optimization and an adaptive finite element scheme, run via OpenMP on a shared-memory system and as tasks on a cluster of identical nodes. The derived cost-accuracy curve for the hybrid FEM suggests a theoretical spatial resolution limit of approximately two Angstroms on a single GPU; however, employing larger cubic supergrids allows for finer discretizations at potentially lower costs. Ultimately, the configuration leveraging a 15x1515 cubic supergrid achieves the highest efficiency-accuracy ratio on a single GPU, surpassing all other methods examined on both single-node and multi-node systems. To facilitate comparisons across different systems, this paper also details a protocol for estimating the cost-accuracy curve for an arbitrary target system. Ultimately, no single method emerges as universally optimal; rather, the choice should depend on the specific requirements of the system under investigation. Ultimately, this work serves as a benchmark for spatial discretization methods in molecular dynamics, providing guidelines for selecting the most appropriate technique for given systems, and highlights the potential of the previously underestimated hybrid FEM for molecular simulations. To aid future comparisons, this research also outlines a procedure for determining the cost-accuracy curve for any desired system, utilizing the contact surface area per atom ($\Sigma/N$) as a proxy for system size. Although deep learning has delivered significant successes in image captioning, the lack of high-quality, large-scale annotated datasets has resulted in generated descriptions that are context-dependent and inconsistent. For visually impaired users, these inconsistencies and inaccuracies in image captions are as problematic as syntax errors in code for programmers; therefore, improved guidelines for image description generation are crucial. While existing datasets like MS-COCO and AISTOR are widely used for training, validating, and evaluating models, their annotation guidelines are either too lenient or simply absent. This paper introduces OpenImagesGuidelines, a comprehensive set of guidelines designed to produce more consistent and descriptive image captions. These guidelines build upon AISTOR's "Five Ws" framework but expand it to cover six key aspects: Who, What, Where, When, Why, and How Many, along with modifiers and sentence structure. We evaluated this new framework using a between-subjects design across two studies. Results indicate that observers can more reliably rank the descriptive quality of images when the guideline is explicitly followed, achieving statistical significance (p < .05) in both Studies 1 and 2. Furthermore, a qualitative analysis suggests that emphasizing the "Why" aspect may not be necessary, as it could introduce irrelevancies into descriptions. Ultimately, OpenImagesGuidelines offer a robust foundation for creating consistent, high-quality datasets for image captioning, benefiting visually impaired individuals, researchers, and models alike. By building upon and expanding the successful AISTOR framework, these guidelines are easily adaptable for other consistency-focused tasks, such as machine translation. Our resources are freely available at https://github.com/williamdavidson/Image-Guidelines.
This study tackles the optimization challenge in quantum field theory, specifically addressing the problem of maximizing a composition of an Euler-Arnold system on a manifold and a monotone function defined on its range. By utilizing the first-order conditions derived from the Euler-Arnold equations and a specific characterization of where the derivative of the monotone function vanishes, we derive a set of algebraic equations. These algebraic formulations allow us to formulate and solve the optimization issue numerically. As a practical application, we consider the $U(1)$-symmetric Scaled Mass Tensor Model (SMMT) and derive the $\beta$-function and mass ratio $\mu$ as polynomials within the gamma-function based amplitude model (GAM). Employing the Newton-Raphson method, we determine the unique real positive solution for GAM's parameter $\lambda$, thereby calculating the $\beta$-function and mass ratio $\mu$ at the physical Z-boson mass $m_Z$. The implications of this solution regarding the running of the mass ratio $\beta(m)$ and its physical significance are also discussed. As the model's name suggests, our approach relies heavily on numerical methods to solve the derived algebraic systems; therefore, this work serves as a foundational step toward a more analytical solution. To facilitate future research, we provide the Python code for our method as open source via GitHub at the following URL: https://github.com/telgars/SDPT3_SMMT.
Heavy quarks, for which the mass satisfies $m_Q\Lambda_{\rm QCD}\gg 1$, interact via QCD and can combine to create a spectrum of heavy quarkonia (two-body $Q\bar Q$ systems) as predicted by nonrelativistic QCD. Beyond these, additional exotic hadrons represent another anticipated domain of QCD existence. Lattice calculations offer a potent tool for validating both nonrelativistic QCD and the notion of exotic hadrons. While calculating two-body bound states on a grid demands fewer computational resources than general hadronic states, it remains a significant challenge. This paper outlines the methodology required to determine three-body heavy hadrons ($HH\bar Q Q$) on lattice grids, potentially enabling such a calculation in the nearest future. Such an endeavor would serve as a valuable test for QCD binding mechanisms and for the concept of exotic hadrons. Furthermore, the configuration space mixing required for this process could be adapted to investigate two-body heavy quarkonia, potentially enabling higher-resolution calculations than currently feasible. Regarding the symbol $D$, it denotes the lattice spacing.
This study investigates the fair-throughput and sum-throughput optimization challenges addressed by users with distinct data demands within a single-source wideband waveforming system. The proposed model accounts for non-orthogonal user access, channel-dependent wideband allocation, and advanced modulation and coding techniques. By integrating game theory and convex optimization, the authors derive the maximum fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Numerical analyses are conducted to evaluate the system's performance under varying constraints, including total wideband resources, user demand distributions, and channel conditions. Additionally, the impact of resource constraints on both fair-throughput and sum-throughput is thoroughly examined. The findings reveal that increasing total wideband resources significantly enhances both metrics. Furthermore, as long as resource constraints remain loose, the source node operates near its optimal wideband allocation; however, under tight constraints, both fair-throughput and sum-throughput decline due to reduced allocation flexibility. Finally, the study compares fixed-wideband and dynamic-wideband strategies across different user demand scenarios to highlight the advantages of dynamic allocation. These insights offer valuable guidance for optimizing wideband resources in single-source multi-user communication networks. Optimization analyses indicate that both fair-throughput and sum-throughput can be enhanced by adjusting wideband allocations, modulation orders, and coding rates. The optimization framework is structured in two phases: initially, users are segmented into groups based on their demand traits and channel qualities using a greedy algorithm; subsequently, uniform wideband resources are assigned to each group. For a given allocation, water-filling optimization determines the optimal coding rate. Numerical methods are employed to assess performance under varying total wideband constraints. As anticipated, expanding total wideband resources significantly improves both fair-throughput and sum-throughput. Furthermore, the proposed non-orthogonal wideband allocation strategy yields higher fair-throughput and sum-throughput than traditional orthogonal allocation, particularly when total wideband constraints are stringent. When constraints are minimal (e.g., 5 MHz), non-orthogonal allocation grants users approximately 6.6 MHz, raising the fair-throughput by over 40 % compared to orthogonal methods limited to 5 MHz. Similarly, sum-throughput increases from 11.3 to 13.3 Mbps. These results underscore the benefits of non-orthogonal wideband allocation, which better leverages limited spectrum resources. The integration of non-orthogonal wideband allocation and adaptive coding rates represents a promising strategy for maximizing throughput in single-source multi-user systems, especially where spectrum is scarce. This study presents a digital copy of the global analysis performed by the JHPULEID collaboration to determine the parton distribution function (PDF) of the proton. Guided by the QCD factorization framework, the analysis involves fitting a comprehensive set of deep inelastic scattering (DIS), inclusive hadron production, and elastic form factor data. Driven by the goal of obtaining a PDF set suitable for quantum electrodynamics (QED)-corrected LUXE (fixed target) predictions at both bootstrapper and boosted crossers energies, we introduce additional observables into the fit, specifically single and inclusive hadron production processes. As expected, the non-QCD dominant photon-to-hadron transition PDF component emerges significantly suppressed at low $Q^2$ but gains importance at higher scales due to its $alpha_QED$ (or $Z$) weighted nature. The final JHPULEID2024 PDF set comprises the proton's $alpha_QED$-corrected sum, difference, and ratio of quark ($q$), anti-quark ($bar{q}$), gluon ($G$), and $Z$-component (defined as $3gluon - 2quark - anti\_quark$) distributions. This set includes the individual $alpha_QED$-corrected distribution functions at the MLLE scale (275 GeV) for the proton, neutron, and nucleus (Li-6 and Li-7), along with their respective $Z$-components. Furthermore, the set features the polarization-dependent helicity distributions ($Delta q$, $Delta G$) derived from a simultaneous fit to current global data, with predictions for future experimental datasets included. This document replaces the earlier JHPULEID2019 (or JHPU) set and supersedes all preceding sets developed by this collaboration. To facilitate the use of the JHPULEID2024 set in other analyses, we provide Python code for its implementation, which can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/JHPULEID/JHPULEID2024. Replacing the traditional CT, MM, ST, and NP PDF sets in other global analyses with the JHPULEID2024 set is straightforward using the supplied conversion code. It is anticipated that this new set will offer benefits in anomaly resolution (such as the $B_s-R_{s}$ and magnetic moment mu), particularly when combined with larger nuclear PDF ratios
Tzeris's optimal control theory was applied to a G/E combustion model within a vortex tube setup to conduct linearized stability analyses of turbulent reacting flows. By deriving the Euler-Cauchy equations for the system's linearized model, researchers evaluated multiple G/E formulations via eigenvalue calculations. The Thomas-Fermi model emerged as the most appropriate for the linearized framework; using this, they re-derived the Sbar and $\Phi$ linearized equations from scratch and compared them with established linearized models found in current literature. This approach offers a rapid method for assessing various linearized models and serves as an effective training exercise for graduate students working with turbulent reacting flows. Additionally, the process involves deriving the energy equation, which provides students practice with vector and tensor algebra. Systems science principles, particularly optimal control theory, can significantly contribute to turbulent flow research, offering frameworks for linearized analyses, eddy viscosity modeling, and filtering techniques used in large eddy simulations. Such systems science approaches also facilitate the development of simplified models for engineering applications. This paper serves both as a practical methodology for evaluating linearized models and as an educational resource for exploring systems science concepts in turbulent flow research. Systems science has historically underrepresented research into turbulent reacting flows, but recent developments suggest it can offer valuable simplified models for engineering use cases, support linearized stability and optimal growth analyses, and facilitate large eddy simulation frameworks. These systems science frameworks can be implemented through modeling, experimental design, and control theory applications. Recent work has explored control theory for turbulent flows using eddy viscosity models for direct numerical simulations and simple shear flows, as well as simplified models for vortex flows. However, these studies have not addressed detailed chemistry models like the Gulari-Erdogan (G/E) model, which tracks mass fractions of species in turbulent flows. This present study investigates the feasibility of a systems science framework for a vortex flow configuration utilizing the G/E detailed chemistry model. The paper begins by briefly outlining systems science concepts relevant to this feasibility study, followed by a review of the G/E model and its adaptation for vortex flows, and concludes with a discussion on control theory applications in this context. Control theory finds extensive use in engineering, particularly in steady-state optimization for processes like chemical plants and dynamic optimization for vehicles and aircraft. In research, control theory aids experimental design, linearized stability analyses, and nonlinear control strategies. Nonlocal gravity models, which introduce spacetime nonlocality to potentially resolve singularity formation in general relativity and attract interest in nonlocal modifications of gravity, require a constitutive relation linking nonlocal variables to observable quantities. However, prior to this work, no constitutive relation had been established for nonlocal extensions of the Arnowit-Dyerlandi-Thorne-Westherhoff (ADMW) formalism, which is widely used in nonlocal gravitational research. This paper derives a constitutive relation for nonlocal ADMW theories, demonstrating how to derive equations of motion for these nonlocal frameworks. We apply this constitutive relation to nonlocal BHT (Behrendsen-Hoelderlein-Tue) and QNRF (quantized nuclear radius function) models, highlighting how the chosen constitutive relation influences their predictions. Additionally, we derive a nonlocal generalization of the BHT master equation and conclude by discussing potential directions for future work. The derived constitutive relation mirrors structures found in effective field theories for solid state physics and nonlocal modifications of gravity; specifically, it relies on cutoff scales and powers of the Laplacian operator. Findings from this study suggest that implementing a constitutive relation in nonlocal ADMW theories could enable nonlocal effects to become significant at specific curvature scales, potentially altering historical curvature trajectories and offering testable outcomes. This work essentially adapts the approach by Boulanger, Westherhoff, and Gamborin (nonlocal modes as effective field theories) to the ADMW framework, suggesting that future investigations into specific nonlocal models should incorporate a constitutive relation analogous to that presented here. Strangeness enhancement in proton-proton (pp) collisions represents a striking phenomenon first observed by Alice at ultra-relativistic LHC energies and subsequently verified across a vast range of center-of-mass energies. This phenomenon has prompted extensive theoretical investigation and will soon enable detailed studies in high-energy pp collisions at the newly constructed High-Luminosity LHC. While quantum chromodynamics (QCD) predicts no such enhancement for hadronic reactions at lower energies, the origin of this effect at ultra-relativistic scales remains enigmatic. Candidate explanations include initial-state parton distribution modifications, final-state multiple parton interactions, and strangeness suppression factor alterations. While none of these mechanisms can stand alone as the definitive cause, recent data from high-energy pion-proton ($\pi$p) collisions suggest that final-state multiple parton interactions offer the most plausible account. Looking forward, detailed measurements of strangeness production at various center-of-mass energies in pp, $\pi$p, and $\pi$\u2014p collisions at the future UltraForward Colliders (UFCh and UFChh) could provide further clarification on this phenomenon and its underlying mechanisms. Given that multiple parton interactions are also anticipated to influence particle production in heavy-ion collisions, a clearer understanding of this effect at lower energies could yield significant insights for heavy-ion physics. Furthermore, the coexistence of final-state multiple parton interactions and strangeness enhancement at lower energies could help resolve the "conical flow" phenomenon seen in proton-lepton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=$2.76 TeV and potentially other energies. An important note is that, due to the scaling of parton distribution functions with energy, multiple parton interactions will diminish at higher energies, implying that strangeness enhancement would likely vanish at ultra-high energies beyond the LHC's capabilities. Conversely, multiple parton interactions at lower energies could be better described by urfon splitting and merging rather than gluon splitting and merging. Ultimately, confirming final-state multiple parton interactions as the source of strangeness enhancement would demand evidence from systematics spanning multiple energy scales, something only feasible with the high statistics achievable at the High-Luminosity LHC and the upcoming UltraForward Colliders.
The existence of neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (NS LMXBs) that spin up to millisecond radio pulsar (MSP) populations is a confirmed phenomenon. These systems accrete from companion stars, and upon ceasing mass transfer, they become MSPs. While most known NS LMXBs are in quiescent states—either because their luminosity falls below detection thresholds or due to intrinsic faintness—intrinsic faintness is typically attributed to sub-Eddington accretion from very low-mass companions. Such masses create tension with the observed MSP spin distributions and the typical ~0.2 solar mass transfers seen in these binaries. This paper demonstrates that a Galactic population of intrinsically "hidden" NS LMXBs with masses around 0.1 solar stars is plausible and necessary to account for the vast number of Milky Way's MSPs, particularly those in the "missing" high-mass gap between neutron stars and black holes. Furthermore, this population aligns with the observed pulsar spin distribution and the overall Milky Way MSP population. Ultimately, these "hidden" binaries represent the ultimate precursors to millisecond radio pulsars. Detecting them remains challenging due to their intrinsic faintness and the lack of optical counterparts, as the donor stars are too cool and low-mass to emit visible light.
We introduce a family of embeddings for bipartite graphs that are "nearly planar," achieved by splitting a minimal set of vertices into multiple nodes. These nearly planar drawings maintain straight-line edges and are constructed in linear time. Although the split vertices will not be straight-line points in the final depiction, we demonstrate how to conceal these artifacts within regions so small they remain imperceptible to human observers. Leveraging this construction, we also define a concept of "nearly planar" drawings for general graphs and provide a construction that maximizes visibility in a bipartite subdivision, subsequently mapping it back to the original graph. Finally, we present a construction for general graphs that produces a planar drawing preserving straight-line edges on a subset of edges, while rendering the remaining edges random without recourse to color coding.
We introduce HyperDegrade, a new efficacy-enhancement technique for Flush+Reload (F&R) privacy attacks. Unlike prior works that optimize specific program regions, HyperDegrade systemically lowers the CPU's time granularity by boosting context-switch frequencies through a custom scheduler and sleep interval adjustments. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that HyperDegrade achieves superior efficacy than previous state-of-the-art solutions across three common workloads: synthetic workflows, CloudWork, and Telemetrics. Specifically, for the synthetic workload, HyperDegrade reduces the mean squared error by a factor of 3x compared to Optimized F&R and by 1.7x relative to Noise. In terms of trace requirements, HyperDegrade needs only 10% as many traces as Optimized F&R to process the synthetic workload, and 2x fewer traces than SleepFurrow. These advantages also hold true for CloudWork and Telemetrics workloads. Furthermore, we evaluate HyperDegrade's efficacy against the SearchRank workload, which previously proved impossible for Optimized F&R to achieve significant improvements over Baseline F&R; HyperDegrade successfully reduces the errors for nine metrics in this workload as well. To assist researchers, we have open-sourced the source code, compiled binaries, configurations, and results for all tested workloads at https://github.com/abhi1901/HyperDegrade.
This paper introduces a set of local moves applicable to diagonal singular curves within $\R^3$ and demonstrates their utility in deforming various knotted structures. Specifically, we utilize these moves to establish the equivalence of two definitions of the crossing number for diagonal singular curves and further derive the invariance of the bridge index, circular chord index, and h index under these transformations when applied to diagonal, satellite, and horizontal singular curves. As an additional contribution, we compute the crossing number and circular chord index for a collection of distinct singular curves detailed in Table~1. These results serve to validate and corroborate findings related to h index inequalities previously reported by the first and third authors in \cite{LBNSW}. Finally, we outline several potential directions for future research. These studies are conducted within the domain of knot theory.
This research investigates how the distribution of task difficulties influences the decision-making strategies of agents facing a public good dilemma modified by an optional exit mechanism. Using an integrated theoretical and empirical framework, the studies reveal that when high-quality completion is demanding, agents are more inclined to abandon the public good initiative to pursue individualistic actions. Conversely, when completion is easier, agents tend to contribute more, shifting responsibility toward free-riders who choose not to exit. Findings indicate that both individual strategies and overall system performance are non-monotonically affected by the variability in task difficulty. These results offer managerial insights into optimizing collective outcomes and enhancing organizational efficiency regarding public goods, suggesting that organizations should avoid concentrating efforts solely on challenging initiatives while ensuring simpler tasks do not receive excessive resources, which could lead to diminishing returns. This study investigates the properties of Cartesian products of functions, addressing the challenge of uniquely expressing any function $f:A\times C\rightarrow B\times D$ in the form $g_1\a g_2\times h_1\big h_2$, where $g_1,h_1:A\rightarrow B$ and $g_2,h_2:C\rightarrow D$. We examine two specific decompositions: the Shortest Cartesian Decomposition (SCD) and the Regular Cartesian Decomposition (RCD). We provide characterizations for the uniqueness of these decompositions and define a method to compute the RCD from the SCD. Furthermore, we analyze the interconnections between the SCD, RCD, and the regular representation. Specifically, we establish a Cartesian counterpart to Diagonal Groups, offering a geometric interpretation for the unique transition between the SCD and the regular representation. To facilitate these investigations, we have developed and open-sourced Python packages dedicated to Cartesian Decomposition, which integrate seamlessly with existing libraries for permutation groups and function analysis. These tools enable the study of Cartesian Decomposition in relation to Permutation Groups, Image Groups, and Tensor Decomposition. The packages are accessible at https://github.com/JamieFutcher/CartesianDecomposition.
Sloshing-Sagnac interferometers represent a novel configuration derived from the standard Sagnac setup, offering enhanced sensitivity to the Special Relativistic Sagnac Effect and interferometric back-action. This study employs a multi-parametric fitting approach to optimize a sloshing-Sagnac system under broad operational conditions. We confirm the formation of Ramsey fringes and a nearby Kondo point, exhibiting characteristics akin to those found in Michelson and Michelson-Sagnac hybrid interferometers. Furthermore, we verify the hyperbolic response curve typical of Sagnac systems. Notably, we observe a sensitivity increase by a factor of 11.2 relative to the conventional Sagnac design and 10.6 compared to the Michelson configuration. These findings indicate that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer serves as an effective platform for exploring various interferometric effects and holds promise for applications in rotation detection and gravitational wave observation. As a scalable architecture, it could potentially surpass the sensitivity limits of current third-generation gravitational wave detectors. To facilitate future optimizations and rotation sensing applications, we derive an optimal operating point and its corresponding sensitivity formula. Additionally, we introduce a "stepped-optimal" optimization strategy aimed at overcoming quantum shot-noise constraints.
This study introduces NOVR-XL, an enhanced random access (RA) protocol designed to mitigate the near-far effect and boost RA performance in extreme-large multiple access (XL-MA) systems. The proposed scheme involves the far user requesting an extended pilot training duration to enable the base station (BS) to locate the user's position and adjust its beamforming for improved signal reception during message training and decoding phases. Simulation results demonstrate that NOVR-XL significantly outperforms existing RA schemes across a wide range of system parameters, with coverage probability (CP) and successful access probability (SAP) gains reaching up to $O(10\times)$ and $O(100\times)$, respectively. Furthermore, the simulations indicate that NOVR-XL delivers superior CP and SAP even when the number of antenna elements in the XL-MIMO system exceeds $10^3$. These findings confirm that NOVR-XL is a viable solution for real-world XL-MIMO deployments. To further validate these conclusions, the study provides geometric probability analyses for NOVR-XL and conducts comprehensive comparisons between NOVR-XL, NOVR, and conventional RA schemes using tractable bounds and Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, the numerical analyses explore the impact of key system parameters on CP and SAP, offering practical guidance for optimizing deployment configurations. The authors hope these insights assist in the practical implementation of XL-MIMO and XL-MA technologies. Notably, this work represents the first application of real-world trace data to analyze the scalability of scalability-based techniques in XL-MIMO systems.
Neural language models are renowned for their superior performance in various natural language processing applications, including machine translation and textual entropy task prediction. However, N-gram models continue to deliver competitive results, particularly when hybridized with neural approaches. This study introduces a novel hybrid architecture designed for textual entropy prediction, building upon a predetermined N-gram to neural network framework by incorporating an attention mechanism and multiple sentence-level features. Experimental results from multiple multi-task datasets demonstrate that our new model achieves comparable or superior outcomes to existing methods. Furthermore, findings indicate that the proposed architecture performs effectively even with sparse data; for instance, in the low-resource Low-German Sentiment dataset, the model improved outcomes by up to 13 ranks compared to the baseline. Ultimately, these results suggest that traditional N-grams remain a valuable component in combined systems for both low-resource and high-resource environments. Leveraging the differences between N-gram and neural models enables the hybrid system to learn patterns that single models might miss, leading to overall improved performance. These conclusions align closely with those observed in machine translation. Future work will explore adding more external features and investigating the impact of varying N-gram orders (e.g., Bi-gram or Auto-gram) on model efficacy. By combining N-gram and neural components, this approach has proven successful across multiple processing types, such as sentiment analysis and topic classification. Consequently, this framework can be adapted for other language tasks, offering a cost-effective solution for processing images and audio. Furthermore, utilizing N-grams as a baseline before incorporating neural elements may help optimize training time and computational resources. Despite these advantages, questions remain regarding why specific combinations of N-gram orders and components yield better results than others, as well as which configurations work best for different datasets and tasks. Answering these inquiries could guide the selection of optimal settings for specific processing scenarios. Additionally, replacing N-grams with other static statistics, such as character $N$-grams or context vectors, represents another promising area for future investigation.
This study presents an enhanced optical character recognition (OCR) system designed to count votes via text input from photos taken at polling stations, a solution relevant for elections in developing nations where resources are limited. Because OCR is highly sensitive to noise, we integrated a spell correction algorithm to improve accuracy. The proposed pipeline utilizes a neural OCR model, USTTCL-Urdu, to convert image input into text, which the spell corrector then processes before a final vote tally is generated. As the system relies on user-captured images, noise sources include camera-induced artifacts, environmental lighting, and operator errors like blur or shake. Given that most votes are cast for few candidates, we incorporated a context-based correction algorithm to leverage grammatical and situational clues for converting noisy text to the correct characters. By optimizing this context-based method with a genetic algorithm, we achieved near-perfect correction for homogeneous and few-shot contexts. Our experiments with this optimized pipeline on a real-world dataset show the system is practical for actual elections; notably, the USTTCL-Urdu OCR model reached 90.02% accuracy, and the overall pipeline achieved 89.08% accuracy. Introducing the context-based genetic algorithm correction raised the USTTCL-Urdu model's performance to 96.61%, and the complete pipeline achieved 91.56% accuracy. Furthermore, we conducted tests on the Zulu and Urdu languages to verify the solution's applicability across different linguistic contexts. The source code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/SaadIqbal99/VOtE and http/VOteCountingDataset/.

Baroclinic storms represent the predominant weather phenomenon in an Earth-like atmosphere, giving rise to familiar extratropical cyclones and associated deep convection. While baroclinic instability has been identified in the Martian atmosphere, atmospheric rotation on Mars is substantially weaker than on Earth, and its horizontal scale remains uncertain. This study employs a two-dimensional, dry, inviscid, ideal-gas numerical model to investigate a Martian basic state mirroring present-day conditions, subject to an initial perturbation analogous to a mature baroclinic storm. The resulting evolution is compared against a corresponding Earth-like simulation. Despite significant differences in physical parameters, the Martian simulation exhibits several circulation features similar to those on Earth, including scale adjustment, potential vorticity inversion, frontogenesis, and wave cyclonic/anticyclonic splitting. These findings suggest that baroclinic storms on Mars share fundamental characteristics with extratropical cyclones on Earth. However, the weak rotation on Mars limits these storms' ability to develop a warm core, vertically tilt their circulation, or reach a rapid intensification stage. These results align with previous research on Martian baroclinic instability and suggests that future observations of Martian winds and clouds during storms should focus on detecting these fundamental traits.

This study addresses the long-standing challenge of determining the true magnetic flux fraction ($\alpha_\mathrm{ph}$) within the photosphere of active regions, a parameter critical for reliable vector magnetic field measurements and overall solar physics research. While previous methods relied on fitting synthetic spectra to observed LOS (Line-of-Sight) data using model atmospheres with a single, region-wide $\alpha_\mathrm{ph}$, we propose a novel approach that explicitly incorporates spatial variations in the magnetic fill fraction directly into the inversion algorithm. Utilizing a Bayesian framework, we derived the vector magnetic field, thermal structure, and spectral response functions (SRFs) for a large, $\beta-$gamma emitting active region using an Inverse Kinematic Source Inversion (iKSI) method that accounts for this explicit magnetic fill fraction variation. The resulting map, which captures the explicit fill fraction variation ($\alpha_\mathrm{ex}$), was then compared against a conventional solution ($\alpha_\mathrm{ph}$) derived via a standard non-linear least squares (nLLS) inversion. Our analysis demonstrates that the explicit fill fraction map ($\alpha_\mathrm{ex}$) aligns significantly better with the LOS SRF than the traditional single-value solution ($\alpha_\mathrm{ph}$), particularly in $\delta$-structured areas, without degrading the fit to other solar parameters. Furthermore, we observe a strong correlation between $\alpha_\mathrm{ex}$ and the $\delta$-structure, as well as between $\alpha_\mathrm{ex}$ and the magnetic fill fraction derived from UV 121\AA\ spectroheliograms, a finding that supports recent conclusions from 121\AA\ image analyses regarding significant spatial variations in the magnetic fill fraction. This work represents the first application of an inversion technique that explicitly varies the magnetic fill fraction, offering a substantial advancement over previous "hidden assumption" methods like nLLS and MLEM. We anticipate that this new technique will become standard practice, leading to more accurate vector magnetic field maps and enhancing solar physics studies, particularly those focused on solar flares and coronal mass ejections. These findings also hold relevance for astrophysical research concerning magnetic reconnection and its various manifestations. This study investigates whether neural models trained on if-then relation extraction (IftIt) benefit from the hierarchical organization of relation types. We first establish a comprehensive hierarchy for the CommonSenseReasoning (CSM) dataset, dividing 246 if-then relations into 16 broader categories. Subsequently, we train two neural models—DistilBERT-CRIF and TACK—to extract if-then relations from the hierarchical structure down to specific relation pairs. Comparative analysis between training on hierarchical versus flat structures reveals that models trained on the hierarchy consistently achieve higher F1-scores across most specific if-then relations, particularly when moving from broader to narrower categories. These findings indicate that leveraging a hierarchical framework is both practical and effective for if-then relation extraction, warranting further exploration of its structural benefits. Additionally, the complete commonSenseReasoning hierarchy, organized from general to specific if-then relations, is available at: https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/u/0/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fus%2Egooglecom%2Fsheets%2Fd%2F1WI%2Fn%2Fedit%3Fhxid%3D0%26gid%3D911053333#gid%3D911053333.

For instance, determining whether a hospital or a doctor is at fault for a patient's injury is often difficult, as the same event can be framed to imply blame toward either party. This paper introduces a dataset of 1,000 if-then relation pairs derived from Wikipedia's "Adverse event" topic cluster, designed to help language models distinguish between cause and blame relations. We detail the data collection process, present initial findings on how various models perform with this new dataset, and discuss potential applications of the if-then relation data. This work introduces a linear model for viewing synthesis that learns a camera-invariant dual representation alongside a camera-specific primal representation. While the primal components are learned directly from video data, the dual components are derived by solving a structured low-rank decomposition problem. To facilitate this decomposition, we propose a novel regularization term that integrates three regularizations: L1 sparsity, low-rank constraints, and cone constraints. Numerical results demonstrate that this hybrid approach outperforms existing methods, achieving superior viewing synthesis quality. Furthermore, the framework enables efficient novel viewpoint prediction through a simple linear combination of the dual representation and a single scalar. This lightweight design allows the system to be deployed on resource-constrained devices for real-time, safe driving assistance. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/TheoDao/ViewSynthesis.
Different from existing methods, our approach offers a concise viewing synthesis framework superior in both performance and speed, facilitating real-time applications, such as safe driving. To achieve this, we learn a decomposable representation (primal and dual) for viewing synthesis. Specifically, we formulate a large-scale structured low-rank decomposition problem, addressing it via an equivalent constrained optimization model. We derive a closed-form solution for the low-rank representation and introduce a regularized objective function combining L1, low-rank, and cone regularizations. Since this objective is non-convex and lacks a direct closed-form solution, we transform it back into a structured low-rank decomposition model and solve it using an alternating algorithm that optimizes the low-rank representation and a factor matrix alternately. Regularizations guide the low-rank representation toward a structure suitable for viewing synthesis. Finally, we derive a lightweight representation for novel viewpoint prediction by combining the dual representation with a scalar. Numerical results show our method surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the lightweight novel viewpoint representation facilitates efficient viewing synthesis, as demonstrated by our experiments. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the viewing synthesis problem and its mathematical model. Section 3 details the proposed regularized optimization model and its solution. Section 4 provides numerical results, and Section 5 concludes the study.

This study examines the metric dimension of $G$, the truncation by distance $t$ of a connected graph $n$-ordered by its metric (shortest path) distance. We introduce and analyze the function $d(n,t)$, representing the maximum dimension under these constraints. While the metric dimension varies wildly for standard graphs, we demonstrate that $\log_t d(n,t)$ scales linearly with $\log_2 n$. Furthermore, we precisely determine $d(n,t)$ for specific $(n,t)$ pairs, deriving an explicit formula for $d(n,\lfloor n/e\rfloor)$. Additional asymptotic results are derived for the case where $t$ is proportional to $n$. These findings highlight why the metric dimension remains bounded for trees and path graphs but exhibits significant variability in general graphs. Finally, we explore the truncation dimension $i_d(n,t)$, defined as the difference between the metric dimension of $n$ and its truncated version, establishing lower bounds and providing exact calculations for specific scenarios. As with the metric dimension, we determine the behavior of the truncation dimension at its peak. These conclusions extend to the characteristic polynomial of the truncation dimension, which we also analyze. Throughout the research, we provide multiple illustrations to clarify key findings. Additionally, we consider the isometry between the metric spaces of $n$ and its truncation, offering a lower bound for isometries on the geodesic boundary and deriving an exact value for $d(n,2)$. Regarding the relationship between the metric dimension and Gromov's notion of geometric dimension (isoperimetric codimension), we derive a lower bound for the latter based on the former and establish its exact value for $d(n,\lfloor n/e\rfloor)$. To further investigate the isoperimetric properties of the metric space $n$, we define a discrete Laplacian operator, deriving its spectrum under the assumption that $n$ forms a metric ball space.
This study introduces a novel framework to enhance phonocardiogram (PCG) noise reduction and anomaly detection in the presence of real-world noise. Unlike traditional methods that rely on fixed noise models, we tackle the challenge of reducing unknown noise types. To address this, we first train a generative model to learn a latent representation of diverse noise types via a neutralization network. This model serves as a prior for a Bayesian approach, which dynamically estimates noise types and removes them from target PCG signals using the learned latent distribution and a neutralization network conditioned on the specific noise type. We validate the proposed method, termed Bayes-PCG-RN, against multiple existing techniques across two public datasets. Results demonstrate that our method significantly improves PCG noise reduction by large margins. Furthermore, when applied prior to anomaly detection, Bayes-PCG-RN yields superior performance: the model accurately identifies cardiac abnormalities with high precision, particularly in noisy environments, as evidenced by the best F1-score achieved on the PUCPR dataset under various noise types ($\text{F1}_{\text{test},\text{WN}} = 0.89$, $\text{F1}_{\text{test},\text{BA}} = 0.84$, $\text{F1}_{\text{test},\text{TR}} = 0.86$, $\text{F1}_{\text{test},\text{WC}} = 0.82$). The source code for this method is accessible at https://github.com/hnghoangt/Bayes-PCG-RN.
This study examines the CI (neutral carbon) spectral line ratios $R_1=T(3-2)/T(2-1)$ and $R_2=T(2-1)/T(1-0)$ across a sample of extreme starburst galaxies, to assess the extent of their ionized molecular gas reservoirs. The samples analyzed include the CN-15 sample (15 most massive starbursts), STARFORM (a diverse set of gas-rich starbursts), and ALFAMA (local starbursts within 100 Mpc). These observations are compared with simple two-phase thermodynamic models consisting of dense molecular cloud phase (T$_{cc}$) and low-density molecular wind/reservoir phase (T$_{rr}$), while accounting for kinetic temperature effects. In all three samples, the CI line ratios display a clear, monotonic increase from the main sequence toward the sequoia subsample, indicating the presence of larger T$_{rr}$ reservoirs. However, no correlation exists between the R1 and R2 ratios for the CN-15, ALFAMA, or total samples. For the CN-15 sample, the R2 ratio shows a weak correlation with metallicity (Z/Z$_\odot$), with lower R2 values associated with higher Z/Z$_\odot$. Furthermore, the CI flux relative to the IR [3.6] flux ($F_{CI(1-0)}/F_{IR[3.6]}$) exhibits strong correlations with both SFR/M$_\odot$ and SFR/DLINo, mirroring trends seen in the CO-to-FIR conversion factor, yet remains uncorrelated with $R_1$ or $R_2$. These findings suggest that the R1 and R2 ratios are poorly suited for detecting low-density molecular winds or circumgalactic reservoirs in extreme starbursts, likely due to the wide separation between the dense cloud and diffuse reservoir temperatures. Consequently, other tracers such as dust emission should be preferred for identifying these low-density molecular gas components. This conclusion warrants further verification using more sensitive, large-scale observations like those from the future SKA. The raw data for the IRAC, ARMAS, CI(1-0), CI(2-1), CI(3-2), CO, and FNU samples, along with the analysis code, are publicly accessible at https://github.com/ndnelson1990/CI_ratios.

It is established that, in both scenarios, the velocity distribution is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure for any positive time $t>0$ when starting from step dynamics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, as $t\to\infty$, the velocity distribution converges to a singular distribution determined by the entry/extraction rates along the natural order. From this, we deduce that, in the full space setting, a second class particle cannot maintain a linear trajectory for an extended period. Finally, we address the inquiry posed in \cite{LLY21} regarding whether, under symmetric step dynamics in a half-space, a second class particle can follow the boundary for infinitely long; we provide a counterexample showing this is not necessarily true. Along the way, we also present a result indicating that, in a half-space with symmetric step dynamics, a second class particle tracing the boundary behaves, in terms of its velocity distribution, identically to one moving linearly in the full space.

We report the observations of a turning point in the evolution of the NUV-r color with respect to the stellar mass for galaxies with $log(M_{\star})>10.5$ $M_{\odot}$, a trend previously noted in $g-r$ and $r-z$ colors by Labbé et al. (2013). This phenomenon, which we term the "UV turnover," persists across redshifts up to $z=2$ and remains constant over time. While the specific mass where this occurs shifts with redshift, the amplitude of the turnover increases as redshift rises. Although star formation suppression due to bulge growth and buckling offers a plausible explanation for this behavior, additional mechanisms must be involved, as the effect is most pronounced in systems that will not reach the supermassive black hole densities required for tidal disruption. Given that the UV turnover marks the transition from massive to very massive galaxies, it serves as a significant indicator for studying black hole growth and the associated accretion history. Furthermore, since the stellar mass at which the UV turnover happens varies with redshift, it could help resolve discrepancies regarding the peak of the black hole - $M_{\star}$ scaling relation and its evolution. Finally, cosmological simulations need to account for the UV turnover to accurately model the UV luminosity function and its evolution, particularly at higher redshifts where the number density of $log(S_{\nu})\approx-20$ sources is most sensitive to the stellar mass at which the UV turnover arises. Multinational sentiment analysis is a crucial application of NLP that encompasses both cross-lingual and multi-task learning. While deep learning has delivered significant advances in single-task single-language sentiment classification, advancing multi-task multi-language systems to reach peak single-language performance requires careful consideration of training data volume and model architecture. This paper presents a solution for multi-task multi-language sentiment classification designed to maximize performance with minimal training sets. We extend existing cross-lingual models by introducing a "language-independent" hierarchy within convolutional and recurrent layers. This approach leverages shared features to enhance performance in low-resource languages. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art outcomes across all target languages, particularly when using small training datasets. Furthermore, our framework outperforms other multi-task multi-language approaches, confirming the effectiveness of incorporating multi-source language content. Notably, our system enhances single-task performance even in high-resource languages like English. To facilitate future research, the complete model weights are available for download at https://drive.google.com/open?id=1biXAtJXUwPkKZIyIyINuLYcdyBGst666.
We report the detection of an anomalous, non-standard rotation profile in the short-period variable star KIC 9267654 (7.5 \, {\rm km\,s}^{-1}), a 2.5\,M_{\odot} $\delta$ Scuti star, using high-precision, long-baseline spectroscopic observations from the NIRVANA instrument. These data were analyzed with the HARPS pipeline. Our findings reveal that one hemisphere rotates significantly faster than the other, with a measured differential rotation of $\Delta \Omega \approx 25\%$, contrasting sharply with the typical differential rotation seen in p-mode oscillating stars, which is usually $\Delta \Omega \approx 2\%$ (e.g., Sun-like stars and $\delta$ Scuti stars). Furthermore, the rotation direction differs from that of other $\delta$ Scuti stars. Potential underlying causes for this atypical rotation profile and its axial tilt include recent stellar merger events, non-radiative angular momentum loss mechanisms, or unusual internal angular momentum distribution patterns. To further investigate the most plausible explanation, future studies should focus on determining the precise age of this star and searching for surface chemical abundance anomalies.
Fake news spreads rapidly online, endangering society and eroding trust in media institutions. While deepfake videos constitute a severe form of falsification, textual news remains a prevalent vector for misinformation. Although multimedia forensics methods exist to detect deepfakes, adapting them for textual content often yields suboptimal results. To address this, we introduce FEND, a framework capable of identifying both subtle and egregious fake images and videos. Building on the success of MetaHFD for detecting deepfake faces and videos, our MetaFEND model specifically targets artificially altered TWF (text-wrapped frame) and ZLP (zooming-luminance fluctuation) patterns. These patterns serve as robust features for uncovering fabricated content. Extensive experiments on public datasets demonstrate that MetaFEND surpasses state-of-the-art detection methods. Furthermore, the framework is versatile and can be adapted to other forensic features for effective fake news detection. The source code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/HaoZhou98/MetaFEND. By leveraging artificial alteration patterns, MediaForense has become an influential tool for fact-checking potential fake news. Previously, however, configuring MetaHFD required expert knowledge and was cumbersome. Now, we have developed an automated, user-friendly algorithm for non-experts to easily configure MetaFEND for other artificial alteration patterns. This study aims to enhance fake news detection, assisting in curbing the proliferation of fraudulent information. Additionally, by analyzing artificial alteration patterns, media organizations can be guided toward developing new forensic features for fake news detection.
This study examines Golay complementary array pairs (GCAP) and quaternary Golay complementary array pairs (QGCAP) of dimensions $2\times n$. It is demonstrated that a GCAP of size $2\times n$ yields a QGCAP of the same size if and only if a specific quaternary Golay partition of $\{0,1,2,3\}^ {n-1}$ exists. Leveraging this finding, the paper derives necessary conditions for quaternary GCAP pairs and constructs quaternary Golay array pairs achieving nearly optimal constructions under certain conditions. Furthermore, constructive proofs showing the non-existence of QGCAPs for specific sizes are provided. Leveraging a constructed GCAP, the study also yields a new optimal quaternary quasilong code pair and a constructed QGCAP to create a quaternary Golay array pair with enhanced sidelobe levels. Finally, a quaternary GCAP of size $2\times19$ is converted into a quaternary Quasi-Zone-Plate Quasilong Code Pair (QZQLP) of length 20, which isFeasible for the first time. Key applications of these structures include quaternary Golay radar waveform pairs and code division multiple access systems. Necessary conditions for Quaternary Golay Complementary Array Pairs are denoted as Feasible and Constructible when they satisfy both necessary and sufficient criteria for existence. Leveraging the constructive approach presented here, researchers can systematically explore QGCAPs to identify feasible conditions that remain unconstructed; however, as dimensions increase, this process may demand significant computational resources. Ultimately, it is proven that GCAPs of size $2\times n$ generate a corresponding QGCAP of identical dimensions only when $n$ equals the product of two distinct prime numbers. Furthermore, QGCAPs with dimensions $2\times n$ and $n=2^{k}$$ (where $k\ge2$) do not exist.
Deep learning techniques, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have achieved significant success in medical image analysis. This paper evaluates a CNN's capability for directly segmenting regions of interest (RS) within dental X-rays to detect caries. The evaluation involves comparing multiple CNN architectures against a support vector machine (SVM) using a publicly accessible dataset of 17,000 bit-map dental X-ray images. Alongside standard segmentation metrics, the study assesses the confidence levels associated with the network's predicted segments. The results indicate that the CNN surpasses the SVM across all standard metrics when utilizing the preprocessed public dataset. Furthermore, when applied to a separate, unprocessed test set, the CNN not only exceeds the SVM's performance but also generates more precise segments for the most challenging cases. Additionally, the network identifies a higher number of caries lesions than were manually segmented by experts in the test dataset. The source code for the examined network is accessible via https://github.com/bjoernroth/CNN-DSPL. As a regression-based approach, this method offers a rapid, cost-effective solution for locating caries in unknown X-rays, facilitating the development of intelligent systems capable of segmenting and quantifying other anatomical structures in medical images.
We introduce a hierarchical feature extraction framework designed to tackle both unsupervised and supervised tasks, operated via a two-stage process. Initially, an open-set feature space is constructed in an unsupervised manner through a dictionary-based approach that integrates structural information, statistical properties, and sample images. Subsequently, this space is refined using supervised methods to perform classification. To validate this framework, we evaluate it against two standard benchmarks: the AD dataset for anomaly detection and SVHN for classification. Our results surpass current state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating that leveraging structural, statistical, and image-based features together yields superior performance compared to using singular features independently. Furthermore, these findings suggest that anomaly detection and classification can be effectively addressed within a unified framework. Additionally, these outcomes indicate that separating anomaly detection from classification is unnecessary. Finally, to further validate these conclusions, we evaluate the framework on a real-world industrial application focused on printed circuit board defect detection. This study confirms the effectiveness of unifying anomaly detection and classification, potentially eliminating the need for separate solutions. These findings also highlight that unsupervised and supervised feature extraction can be harmonized within a single framework. Notably, existing literature has not previously explored this specific combination of techniques. Our results further suggest that supervised feature extraction does not require data sets excluded from the main corpus, contradicting common assumptions. Finally, our findings indicate that anomaly detection and classification need not rely on disjoint sets of tasks, datasets, or techniques, as previously believed in existing literature. These conclusions challenge multiple common misconceptions found in current research.
Although knowledge graphs are extensive, structured repositories of world knowledge widely used across industry and research, their direct application to textual content remains underexplored. This investigation evaluates the performance of language models when trained on knowledge graph data versus conventional text-based datasets using factual question-answering as a benchmark. Our findings indicate that models trained on knowledge graph information perform comparably to those using traditional data when handling questions directly grounded in the specific knowledge graph they were trained on. However, this advantage disappears when the models are tested on questions concerning content outside that graph's scope. Although this limitation is expected, it is concerning for real-world scenarios involving open-domain factual query answering. To address this, we introduce TRICK, a method that fuses knowledge graphs and contextual passages to answer queries. Experimental results demonstrate that TRICK significantly surpasses state-of-the-art systems across multiple benchmark datasets, including TREC, MLQA, SQuAD, and FEQA. Additionally, we assess TRICK on the WikiHop dataset, a complex question-answer-b triple set based on knowledge graphs, where it achieves near-perfect accuracy. Finally, we extend TRICK to large language models, coining it BIG-TRICK; these models also show marked improvements over current large-scale pre-trained language models across all evaluated datasets. Our source code and dataset resources are accessible at https://github.com/huawei-noah/Transformers/tree/noah-transformers/examples/trick.

Optical tomograms constitute a genuine and intuitive graphical technique for representing quantum states, effectively bridging the gaps between various quantum descriptions and facilitating the detection of nonclassical features. This study introduces two novel measures for entanglement variation, termed the total entanglement change (TEC) and entanglement change density (ECD), extended to optical systems through nonlocal optical tomograms. These metrics highlight nonclassical shifts even in scenarios where the total entanglement remains constant, suggesting they serve as a superior tool for tracing nonclassical transformations. We demonstrate these concepts using specific examples derived from local transformations, Schrödinger-cat states, and squeezed-state transformations. Furthermore, we establish several previously unreported nonclassicality conditions based on nonlocal optical tomograms, offering enhanced criteria for identifying entangled quantum states within hybrid quantum systems. The findings presented herein introduce new methods for characterizing nonclassicality and tracing entanglement dynamics, which are essential for advancing quantum information science and related fields.

Quantum mechanics has revolutionized our understanding of nature, bringing with it the concept of nonclassicality, which signifies deviations from classical physics and its limitations. Entanglement, a hallmark of nonclassicality in quantum mechanics, has been extensively investigated as a resource for quantum information science. Significant advancements have occurred in demonstrating nonclassicality and entanglement across various quantum systems, including mechanical oscillators, atomic ensembles, optical fields, and electromagnetic fields in cavities. These developments have enabled the exploration of nonclassical effects, such as squeezing and entanglement changes, in previously unexpected scenarios. For instance, squeezing has been observed in mechanical oscillators, atomic ensembles, and optical fields, while entanglement changes have been demonstrated in squeezed vacuum beams, mechanical oscillators, and optical-field systems. These achievements have fueled interest in defining and quantifying nonclassical effects and entanglement dynamics, which are crucial for developing quantum protocols and technologies like quantum cryptography, computing, communication, sensing, and metrology.

This study conducts an all-order uncertainty analysis for the branching fraction of the $\bar{B}^0\to K^{*0}\ell^+\ell^-$ decay across selected regions. The findings indicate that quantum chromodynamics (QCD) uncertainties are substantial in the low angular and forward-backward asymmetry domains, yet these become negligible in regions with large $|A_{\rm FB}|$ and $\alpha_2$. These conclusions are validated by comparing predicted asymmetries with experimental data. Furthermore, an optimized choice of quantum chromodynamic uncertainties yields a branching fraction determination that is both more precise and accurate, aligning better with the experimental measurement; for $\bar{B}^0\to K^{*0}\ell^+\ell^-$, this represents an improvement of approximately 20\%. These methods and outcomes are extended to other non-Belle experimental decay regions, and a revised world average is calculated incorporating these updated theoretical errors, which may prove valuable for resolving puzzles related to angular anomalies and lepton universality. To facilitate this, the authors provide a public Python package, \texttt{BelleBrUnc}, designed for quickly estimating Belle II branching fraction uncertainties.
This paper introduces a novel approach to determining the submodule lattice of a multiplicity free $G$-module $V$. The method begins by identifying all potential composition factors that could exist within a specific nonempty interval within the submodule lattice. Leveraging the fact that $V$ is multiplicity free, these factors are arranged into a multiplicity free module comprising all composition factors up to a chosen height; this construct is termed the "ladder" of $V$ at that height. By recursively applying this process, combined with knowledge of the immediate sublattices at each level, the full lattice can be reconstructed. To demonstrate this technique, we calculate the submodule lattice for a extensive collection of minimal nonmultiplicity free modules, utilizing LieTune parameters and irreducible highest weight modules for classical groups detailed in the work of Diener, Diener, King, and Schoonen. Furthermore, we establish that for classical groups, these high-dimensional modules can be replaced with lower dimensional varieties defined by the same LieTune parameters, through the application of branching rules. Specifically, for the symmetric group $S_n$, we prove that varieties corresponding to the same LieTune parameters form a multiplicity free set of representations within the classical group $Sp(2n,\mathbb{F}_q)$, provided $q$ is sufficiently large relative to $n$. We also examine the classical groups $SU(p,q)$ and $F_4(q)$, determining varieties for $Sp(10,\mathbb{F}_q)$ and $F_4(2)$ that satisfy specific geometric constraints but fall outside any previously identified variety hierarchy. Finally, we apply this framework to clarify an explicit variety defined by Laborde and Testut for $F_4(2)$.

We further derive the corresponding explicit constant for the Chebotarev density theorem within the same function field context. Additionally, we establish the explicit version of Chebyshev's bias for this setting and obtain an explicit remainder term for Prime Number Theorem-related results in $\mathbb{F}_q[t]$. Additionally, we outline a plan to adapt these results for $A=\mathbb{F}_q[[t]]$ (the local field context) and discuss potential extensions to global fields of characteristic zero, such as $\mathbb{Z}[$root-n$]$. Ultimately, these findings serve as a foundational step toward rendering remainder terms explicit in the context of number fields.
This work addresses the inquiry posed by John, Sideris, and Yau regarding the existence of classical blow-up solutions to the Schrödinger equation within domains featuring boundaries. Specifically, we derive an optimal smoothing estimate for solutions to $u_t = \Delta u + |u|^{p-1}u$ on such domains, accounting for a nonnegative boundary potential. By combining this estimate with concavity arguments, we establish global existence for sub-critical powers. Furthermore, utilizing the smoothing estimate alongside a fractional derivative loss method, we prove blow-up for the Schrödinger equation with a boundary when the nonlinearity is super-critical. Finally, we provide a fractional derivative loss estimate for solutions operating in the traceless Sobolev space.

The findings indicate that smoothing estimates serve as a potent alternative to classical local well-posedness methods when dealing with nonlinear Schrödinger equations in domains with boundaries. These results align with recent work by Sire and Vial, who derived a similar loss of derivatives estimate in $C^{k,\alpha}$ spaces; however, to our knowledge, this represents the first derivation of such a loss of regularity in standard Sobolev spaces for non-linear Schrödinger equations subject to boundary conditions.

While binary hypothesis testing addresses the simplest scenario, real-world applications often involve selecting one from multiple hypotheses, commonly framed as utility-maximizing detection. Building on these random variables, we explicitly formulate utility functions for detection, sampling, and delaying, incorporating threshold constraints to handle multiple hypothesis selection. Specifically, we propose a generalized "sawtooth" utility function at the threshold boundaries. As a case study, we examine a uniform prior belief across three hypotheses with concave-then-convex utility functions, defining three distinct regions: low, middle, and high. This study presents DiscSense, a comprehensive dataset engineered to evaluate the semantic relatedness of discourse markers. While existing resources primarily focus on classifying the types of semantic relations connecting clauses within specific contexts—often through multiway structures like discourse trees—our approach targets the calculation of a semantic distance between two distinct discourse marker sets associated with equivalent semantic relations. To construct DiscSense, we adapted the OpenSubtitles dataset, which was previously utilized to develop SenseAwars for dialogue acts. By leveraging contextual information from a dual-clause subset of OpenSubtitles and employing the DIARNS system to identify semantic relations, we created a tripleset format comprising: 1) the subtitle context, 2) the discourse marker in the first clause, and 3) the discourse marker in the second clause. Furthermore, we integrated a fourth element, the distributed Wn 8888 relation type, into these triples. Finally, we generated a set of contexts for which two potential semantic relations could be assigned, forming the dualset used for training, training and testing evaluation tasks. The resulting dataset contains 10,000 triplesets and 2,000 dualsets. We assessed the quality of the discourse marker semantics within the dualset T10000 using the Msvo system, utilizing both the overall relatedness score and a classification task to identify semantic relation types. Findings from this evaluation are compared against those from a similar task conducted on a classical set of examples derived from the Discourse wiki (Diw). Additionally, we conducted a cluster analysis based on the top 100 most frequent discourse marker pairs in our dataset, examined through the Msvo system. This analysis aimed to verify whether the system can distinguish between equivalent contexts with differing semantic relations. Last but not least, we administered the dualset T2000 as a test collection for humans and two machine systems, evaluating all three participants using a correlation-based metric. Results from both the cluster analysis and the test collection study demonstrate that the Msvo system is capable of differentiating between equivalent contexts involving diverse semantic relations. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/luiscastro1/DiscSense. This resource will prove invaluable for further research on discourse markers and semantic relations, particularly regarding the evaluation of machine systems operating over Markov contexts.

By analyzing the segments of this source imaged through the LEO, the azimuthal rotation angle serves to identify the specific segments under observation, while the radial translation distance determines the corresponding focal length. Utilizing this method, we precisely calibrated both the focal lengths and field-of-view angles for all segments in a custom-built LEO system. The results demonstrate that this simple geometric source yields highly accurate calibration, with a focal length resolution of approximately 0.5 mm and an angular resolution of about 0.05 degrees. This passive calibration approach offers simplicity and convenience, making it particularly suitable for rapidly verifying the image quality of LEOs before deploying them to measure celestial brightness distributions. Furthermore, the coordinate systems established during calibration facilitate the integration of segment-specific spectral data to construct comprehensive two-dimensional or three-dimensional sky maps for unknown regions. As a passive solution requiring an on-site bright source, this method complements active calibration techniques that utilize known astronomical targets, together ensuring high precision for various LEO applications. Leveraging the segmented imaging characteristic of LEO, this study represents an initial effort to clearly define the optical axes of all segments within a multi-focal-length LEO system, thereby enabling precise localization of astronomical targets across its wide field of view. Such capability is essential for tasks like monitoring variable sources, locating transient events, and mapping celestial brightness distributions.

Atomic interferometry represents the most sensitive detection method for local magnetic fields, achieving sensitivity within an atomic well-gas of approximately $10^{-14}$ G/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ over a spatial range of $\lambda/2$, where $\lambda$ is the matter-wave wavelength. While this constitutes an extraordinarily small magnetic field sensitivity per unit area, the total magnetic field sensitivity remains limited by the shallow depth of the atomic well-gas and thus scales linearly with observation time. To overcome this area-limiting factor, we introduce satellite atomic interferometry. This approach employs two atomic well-gases connected by a long matter-wave baseline to enhance total magnetic field sensitivity. For instance, a setup featuring a short baseline of 6 cm and a wavelength of 1 m could reach a sensitivity of $10^{-13}$ G/$\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ in a four-hour run. Such sensitivity is sufficient to probe new physics, specifically light dark photons ($10^{-13} < \gamma < 10^{-11}$) and axion-like particles ($10^{-13} < \Lambda < 10^{13}$ GeV), filling a critical gap between existing laboratory and astrophysical experiments. As an area-based search for dark photons and axion-like particles, atomic interferometry offers distinct advantages over other experimental methods, potentially enabling the detection of these particles in the local galactic halo. Furthermore, atomic interferometry can serve as a complementary technique to other laboratory experiments for exploring physics beyond the Standard Model. To maximize the benefits of atomic interferometry for both magnetic field measurement and new physics searches, modular designs utilizing multiple atomic well-gases and long matter-wave baselines are essential. Such configurations would significantly improve magnetic field sensitivity per unit area and expand the parameter space searchable per unit of observation time. In this report, we detail the principles of atomic interferometry for magnetic field sensing and new physics searches, summarize previous demonstrations and limitations, and propose a feasible implementation of satellite atomic interferometry. We provide an estimated sensitivity for this proposed setup across a range of new physics parameters, illustrate potential applications, and outline challenges and possible solutions for realization. Furthermore, we discuss the unique roles atomic interferometry can play alongside other magnetic field sensors and in the search for dark photons and axion-like particles, aiming to clarify why this method warrants further consideration and investment.
Nonlocal spectroscopic responses to local states are a hallmark of quantum physics, yet they remain difficult to observe in condensed matter systems. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we examined the local 1$d$ spin-orbit coupling (SOC) induced by magnetic adatoms and dimers on the superconducting lead surface. These states, known as Young's Rashba spin-split surface states (YSR), exhibit nonlocal character. Surprisingly, the width of their momentum-space arcs decreases as SOC strength increases, contrasting with the expected linear expansion seen in bulk BCS superconductors and other thin-film systems. Furthermore, we found that the vertical separation between YSR peak positions is not linearly proportional to SOC strength in the lowest-energy state for adatoms, and even reverses direction for certain dimers. These findings challenge conventional BCS understanding and suggest that SOC arises from a complex mechanism involving multiple orbital contributions. In fact, spin-orbit coupling significantly influences the electronic structure of the lead surface, potentially altering how quantum coherence forms in ultra-thin superconducting layers. Such effects could be even more pronounced in two-dimensional materials. To explore these phenomena further, local probes like STM/STS are indispensable.
